target.title: Dashboard: chart widgets + widget authoring SDK
target.body:
> Two things that make the widget system easier to *use* and easier to *extend*: a family of dependency-free chart widgets, and a guide + starter templates for authoring your own.

Closes #101142 and #101141. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review the new `chart.ts` + `docs/`/`examples/` files as the delta.

## What's in this PR

**Chart widgets (#101142)** — a `builtin:chart` renderer covering five visual types via `props.type`: `line`, `bar`, `area`, `sparkline`, `gauge`.
- Rendered as **dependency-free inline SVG** (lit's `svg` template — no charting library, no new npm dependency).
- Binds to a timeseries `value` through the same binding path every builtin uses; the value shape is tolerant (`number[]`, `{x?, y|value}[]`, or `{points:[…]}`) and normalized to a finite `number[]` before drawing.
- Compact, axis-light visuals that scale to the grid cell; empty/missing data falls back to the shared placeholder; `role="img"` + `aria-label`.

**Widget authoring SDK (#101141)** — `docs/plugins/dashboard-widget-authoring.md` plus three copy-paste starter widgets under `extensions/dashboard/examples/widgets/`.
- The guide documents **both** widget paths: builtin renderers (the `renderX(widget, value, ctx) => TemplateResult` contract, and registering a kind in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS` *and* `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN` — which must change together), and sandboxed custom widgets (the `widget.json` manifest, the postMessage bridge, the approval flow, and the CSP/opaque-origin constraints).
- Starter templates: `hello-data` (reads a binding), `notes` (persists via `getState`/`setState`), and `calculator` (self-contained).

## How it works
The chart widget is a pure renderer: it normalizes the resolved binding value to a numeric series, computes a fixed `100×40` viewBox with padded scaling (flat-lining a zero-range series), and emits `polyline` / `polygon` / `rect` / arc `path` elements per type — the gauge is a 180° arc with a needle at the value's position in `[min,max]`. Nothing fetches; the renderer only draws what its binding resolved. The SDK is documentation + example assets only — no runtime code changes.

Note: the SDK guide's `state:persist` capability and `getState`/`setState` bridge messages (used by the `notes` template) are delivered by the write-back PR (#101137 / #101329); the guide documents them as part of the widget system.

This PR adds **no new dependency** — `pnpm-lock.yaml` is unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** The dashboard had only stat-card and table builtins (no way to visualize a trend), and no documented path for contributors or agents to author new widgets. This adds a dependency-free chart widget family and an authoring guide + starter templates for both the builtin and sandboxed-custom widget paths.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → the UI dashboard suite is green (incl. the chart mapping/render suite: normalize shapes, per-type element counts for line/bar/area/gauge, and empty-state); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and oxlint clean. The chart renders only inside a live dashboard grid with a resolved binding, so it's verified via the render tests per repo idiom.

target.title: Dashboard: ops widgets — agent status + approvals queue
target.body:
> The operational half of the builtin set: see what every agent is doing, and act on what's waiting for you — from a dashboard cell.

Closes #101145 and #101144. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `agent-status.ts` + `approvals.ts` and their wiring as the delta.

## What's in this PR

**`builtin:agent-status` (#101145)** — a compact per-agent/session status list: active-run vs idle, current label, and freshness — the "what's everything doing right now?" glance. It binds to the same `sessions.list` data the `sessions` builtin already uses (no new backend), so it live-updates on the existing broadcast path.

**`builtin:approvals` (#101144)** — a pending-approvals queue with Approve/Deny actions, wired end-to-end through the **existing** widget-approval infrastructure from #101098 (`dashboard.widget.approve`): pending `custom:` widgets appear as cards, and a decision dispatches the same client path the Workspaces pending-card uses. The queue arrives via a new `ctx.approvals` source on the builtin context (mirroring the existing `ctx.embed` pattern), because it's in-memory workspace state rather than an RPC binding.

**Scope note (deliberate):** the gateway's exec/plugin approval RPCs (`exec.approval.*`, `plugin.approval.*`) exist and the app shell uses them, but they are operator-scoped and not in the dashboard's read-only binding allowlist (`DATA_READ_RPC_ALLOWLIST`). Widening that allowlist is a security decision we didn't want to smuggle into a widget PR — so this widget covers the dashboard's own approval queue today, and is shaped to take exec/plugin approvals as additional sources the moment maintainers bless that allowlist addition (called out in the module header). That keeps #72545 progressing without expanding any privilege surface.

## How it works
Both widgets follow the established builtin contract (`renderX(widget, value, ctx) => TemplateResult`), registered in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS` + `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN`. Agent-status is a pure mapper over the resolved `sessions.list` value. Approvals renders from `ctx.approvals` (built by the dashboard view from workspace state) and dispatches decisions through the existing, already-authorized `dashboard.widget.approve` method — this PR adds **no new gateway method and no new privilege**.

No new dependency — `pnpm-lock.yaml` unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** There's no cross-agent activity view in the dashboard (#101145 / the #39127–#54577 cluster), and approvals had no dashboard surface (#101144, advancing #72545) — operators had to open each session or wait for the pending-card to appear on the Workspaces tab. This adds two operational builtins: a live agent-status list and an approvals queue with working Approve/Deny.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → 100 passed, including the new suites (status derivation filters + provenance, decision-vocabulary mapping + limit, populated/empty renders, and Approve/Deny wiring asserted against a mocked client dispatching `dashboard.widget.approve`); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and full type-aware oxlint clean; `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/dashboard` green (schema kind additions).

target.title: Dashboard: stateful notes widget — the first consumer of widget write-back
target.body:
> A notes pad on your dashboard that actually saves — and the pattern every stateful builtin after it will follow.

Closes #101146. **Stacked on #101329 (widget write-back)**, which is itself stacked on #101098 — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `notes.ts` + the `buildBuiltinContext` host change as the delta beyond #101329.

## What's in this PR

- **`builtin:notes`** — an editable notes/todo pad. Content hydrates from persisted state on mount and saves on debounced input (~500 ms), so it survives reloads and stays consistent across two open browsers (the write-back broadcast triggers refetch).
- **A host-bound state accessor for builtins** — the piece that makes this safe and reusable. `BuiltinWidgetContext` gains an optional `state` accessor (`get`/`set`), and the dashboard view now builds the context **per widget** (`buildBuiltinContext`), closing over the host's own `widget.id` when it calls `dashboard.widget.state.get`/`.set`. A widget renderer never names a widget id — it can only ever touch its own state. This mirrors the trust model of the sandboxed path in #101329 (parent binds the id), applied to trusted builtins.
- **Graceful degradation** — with no connected client there's no `state` accessor, and the pad renders read-only with a hint instead of silently dropping writes.

## How it works
Builtins render in the trusted Control UI, so they use the write-back gateway RPCs directly rather than the sandbox's postMessage bridge — but the id-binding discipline is identical: the host supplies `widget.id`, never the renderer. The persist test drives the real `buildBuiltinContext` (not a hand-rolled mock) and asserts the RPC receives `{ widgetId: "notes-42", state: … }` — the id-binding itself is under test. State lives in the per-widget jailed store from #101329 (64 KB cap, atomic writes, separate from `workspace.json`).

No new dependency — `pnpm-lock.yaml` unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Operators want a scratchpad/todo on their dashboard, but before write-back (#101137/#101329) any editable widget reset on reload — and there was no pattern for a *builtin* to persist state safely. This adds a stateful notes builtin plus the host-bound per-widget state accessor that makes it (and future stateful builtins) possible.

target.title: feat(dashboard): sandboxed custom widgets + approval flow [3/3]
target.body:
# Sandboxed custom widgets + approval flow (3/3)

> **The dashboard your agent builds with you.** This is the capability nothing else in the ecosystem has: an agent authors a real HTML widget, it renders live inside the operator's dashboard, and it does so inside a sandbox strict enough that independent security review couldn't break out of it. This is the last mile between "the agent describes a dashboard" and "the agent builds it."

![End-to-end: an agent scaffolds a custom revenue-chart widget, a pending-approval card appears, the operator approves it, the sandboxed iframe mounts and renders live data through the bridge, then the human keeps working the composed grid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/dashboard-demo.gif)

*▶ Full-quality recording ([light](https://github.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/releases/download/modular-dashboard-demo-v1/dashboard-demo.mp4) / [dark](https://github.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/releases/download/modular-dashboard-demo-v1/dashboard-demo-dark.mp4)).*

> **Stack note.** This is the top of a three-PR stack (#101094 backend → #101097 UI → #101098 here). The reviewable new work in *this* PR is the sandboxed custom-widget host — ~1,400 lines of source across 9 files, well under VISION.md's ~5K reviewable-line guideline. Because we don't have upstream write access to set GitHub-native stacked bases, all three PRs target `main` with cumulative diffs, so this branch's diff includes #101094's and #101097's commits until they merge to `main` — **review #101094 and #101097 first, then read this PR's `extensions/dashboard/src/{http-route,serve,manifest}.ts` and `ui/src/{components/dashboard-custom-widget,lib/dashboard/bridge}.ts` as the delta.** This same branch is also the full feature end-to-end — check it out to run everything.

## Run the whole thing

Because this PR sits at the top of the stack, checking it out gives you the complete modular-dashboard feature in one branch — no need to assemble the stack yourself:

```sh
gh pr checkout <this-PR-number>       # or: git fetch <fork> feat/modular-dashboard && git checkout FETCH_HEAD
pnpm install && pnpm build
# start the gateway with the dashboard plugin enabled, open the Control UI → the "Workspaces" tab
```

The default **Overview-as-data** workspace renders on first load. Ask an agent (or run `openclaw dashboard tabs create --title Financials`) to build a tab and watch it appear live; scaffold a custom widget, approve it from the pending card, and watch the sandboxed iframe mount. CI runs against this full integration.

## What problem this solves

#101094 and #101097 get an operator most of the way there with a live grid and trusted, built-in widgets — but the actual bet of this whole series is that an agent can build something *bespoke*: a chart, a custom view, a one-off tool, authored on the spot in response to "build me a revenue chart." That means running agent-authored code inside the operator's browser, which is the one place in this series that needs to be provably safe before it ships, not just believed safe.

## What's in this PR

- **Scaffold → pending → approve → mount lifecycle.** An agent (via the `dashboard_widget_scaffold` tool from #101094) creates a widget directory with a manifest and an `index.html`; it enters the registry as `status: "pending"`. A pending widget renders as a placeholder card (name, author, Approve/Reject) — **no iframe is ever created for a pending or rejected widget, on either the client or the server.** Approval routes through the existing plugin-approvals infrastructure as well as an inline Approve button, so it shows up wherever operators already look for approvals.
- **Sandboxed iframe host** (`ui/src/components/dashboard-custom-widget.ts`): `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">` — never `allow-same-origin`, never any other token. The sandbox attribute is treated as a constant, not configuration.
- **A versioned, minimal postMessage bridge** (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/bridge.ts`): the widget can ask for its declared data bindings and a theme snapshot, and — only with an explicit manifest capability plus a per-invocation operator confirm dialog — ask to send a prompt into chat. The parent only ever accepts messages from the exact iframe window it created, only recognizes a fixed set of message types, and only resolves bindings the widget's own manifest declared — a widget cannot request data it wasn't given permission to see.
- **Static-file-only asset serving**: a new unauthenticated plugin HTTP route (necessary — sandboxed frames carry no device token) that serves *only* files inside the widget's own directory, behind a charset check on the widget name, path normalization, and a containment check, with a locked-down `Content-Security-Policy` (including `connect-src 'none'`, so "no network" is structural, not just a convention) on every response. Only `approved` widgets are served at all — pending/rejected widgets 404 server-side, independent of whatever the client does.
- **Theme sync**: widgets receive the Control UI's current theme tokens so agent-authored UI matches the operator's chosen theme (including #99289's light palette) without the widget author having to guess.

## See it

The full scaffold → pending → approve → mount → live lifecycle, one frame at a time:

**1. Pending — the iframe does not exist yet.** A scaffolded widget lands as a placeholder card (name, author, Approve/Reject). No iframe is constructed on the client, and the assets 404 server-side, until an operator approves.

![A custom widget in the pending-approval card: "Revenue Chart — awaiting approval, built by finance agent," with Approve and Reject affordances and no iframe rendered](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/03-financials-pending-approval.png)

**2. Approved and mounted.** After the operator approves, the sandboxed iframe mounts and renders — here an approved custom chart widget on the composed Financials tab, alongside AI-provenance chips and the finance-activity lifecycle feed.

![The composed Financials tab with the approved, sandboxed custom widget rendering a chart, AI-provenance chips, and the Finance Activity lifecycle feed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/04-approved-sandboxed-chart.png)

**3. Live.** A bound value updates in place as the finance agent writes new data — the widget never fetched anything; the parent pushed the resolved binding over the bridge.

![The approved custom widget with a bound revenue value updating live, driven by a data push through the bridge rather than any network call from the widget](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/05-live-revenue-update.png)

The same composed Financials tab in the dark theme, kebab menu open, sandboxed widget rendering — agent-authored UI adopts the operator's theme tokens automatically:

![Dark theme: the composed Financials dashboard with the sandboxed custom widget rendering and a widget cell's kebab menu open](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/100yenadmin/openclaw/d9a7c485270e34d74c19952db8f4d04273d8ed1a/docs/assets/modular-dashboard/financials-composed-dark.png)

## How it works

The design principle is one sentence: **the widget is untrusted agent-authored code, so it gets no origin, no network, no credentials, and no direct line to the gateway — the trusted parent does everything on its behalf.** Every mechanism below is a consequence of that.

### The key insight: the widget never talks to the gateway

A custom widget is HTML/JS an *agent* wrote. It renders in the operator's browser but is treated as hostile. It has no way to reach the gateway: the sandbox denies it an origin, the CSP denies it the network, and it holds no token. All data reaches it through a single narrow channel — the parent resolves the widget's *declared* bindings and posts the results in. If the widget wants data it wasn't granted, there is no request it can make that succeeds. That inversion (parent-resolves-on-behalf, never widget-fetches) is what makes running agent-authored code in the operator's browser defensible.

### Rendering — a constant `allow-scripts` sandbox

The host component (`ui/src/components/dashboard-custom-widget.ts`) mounts `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" referrerpolicy="no-referrer">`. The sandbox attribute is a **constant string**, not configuration — never `allow-same-origin`, never `allow-top-navigation`, `allow-popups`, or `allow-forms`. With `allow-scripts` alone, the frame's origin is opaque (serializes as `"null"`), so it can never touch the parent's storage, cookies, or DOM. The code comments call this out explicitly ("do not templatize") so a future well-meaning edit can't loosen it.

### Serving — a static-only, path-jailed, approval-gated route

Sandboxed frames carry no device token, so the asset route (`extensions/dashboard/src/http-route.ts`) is registered `auth:"plugin"` (unauthenticated). That is safe *only because* the route is static-file-only and can leak nothing:

- **Name and path**: `/plugins/dashboard/widgets/<name>/<path...>` — `<name>` passes the canvas charset check (`^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`); `<path...>` is URL-decoded, logically normalized, and containment-checked against the widget's own directory (the `extensions/canvas/src/documents.ts` idiom, reused verbatim).
- **Every rejection is a 404, never a 403** — a traversal attempt, a bad charset, a disallowed extension, or a non-GET method is indistinguishable from a miss, so the route leaks no existence information.
- **Content type is allowlisted by extension** (html/js/css/json/svg/png/jpg/webp/woff2/txt/md/csv); anything else 404s.
- **Strict CSP on every response**: `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'`, plus `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. `connect-src 'none'` makes "no network" **structural**, not conventional.
- **Approval gate at serve time**: the handler checks the registry and serves *only* widgets whose `status === "approved"`. Pending/rejected widgets 404 server-side, independent of anything the client does — so approval-bypass is enforced where the bytes are, not merely in the UI.

### The bridge — versioned, window-identity-filtered, allowlist-re-checked

Data reaches the widget through a versioned postMessage bridge (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/bridge.ts`, envelope `{ v:1, type, … }`), whose security logic is deliberately DOM-free so it's unit-testable in isolation:

- **Accept filter by window identity**: the parent accepts a message only when `event.source === iframe.contentWindow`. Origin strings are useless here (a sandboxed origin is `"null"`), so identity is the check — a message from any other window, including a second widget's iframe, is dropped.
- **Fixed message set, declared bindings only**: the parent recognizes a closed set of types and resolves only bindings the widget's *own manifest* declared, by `bindingId`. `file`/`static` bindings resolve via `dashboard.data.read` (server re-validates the jail); `rpc` bindings are called by the parent on its own gateway client — and the method is **re-checked at resolve time** against the browser-side mirror of the plugin's write-time allowlist (`RPC_METHOD_ALLOWLIST`), a defense-in-depth check on top of PR1's write-time gate. A widget cannot request a binding or method it wasn't granted.
- **Parent→child posts use `targetOrigin "*"`** (required for an opaque child origin) — acceptable *by construction* because the only payloads ever posted are binding data and theme tokens the widget is already entitled to. No config, no session data, no tokenized URLs are ever sent.
- **`sendPrompt` is triple-gated**: it requires the manifest capability `prompt:send`, then a per-invocation operator **confirm dialog** quoting the exact text, then it's **rate-limited** (1 in-flight + 10/min per widget) before it reaches the existing chat-send path.
- **Theme sync**: `getTheme` returns the Control UI's current CSS custom-property tokens (including #99289's light palette) so agent-authored UI matches the operator's theme without the author guessing.

### Approval lifecycle

An agent-scaffolded widget (`dashboard_widget_scaffold`, from #101094) enters `widgetsRegistry` as `status:"pending"`. A pending widget renders the placeholder card — **no iframe is constructed, client or server**. Approval routes through the existing plugin-approvals infrastructure (so it appears wherever operators already look for approvals) as well as the card's inline Approve button → `dashboard.widget.approve` → re-broadcast. Only `approved` widgets ever get an iframe, and only `approved` widgets are ever served — the gate is double-enforced, UI and server.

### Then we tried to break it

This layer got an independent adversarial security review before being proposed here, specifically because it's the highest-security-surface part of the project. The review's job was to try to refute three claims — the path-jail on asset serving, the iframe sandbox, and the CSP — and it could not refute any of them, across two independent passes and dozens of live probes against the running implementation (path traversal variants, encoded/absolute/backslash/symlink-out paths, sandbox-attribute inspection, and a live `connect-src 'none'` network test).

The review did find one real gap: a prompt-dispatch rate limit that didn't survive a widget being removed and re-added (a remount could reset the counter). That was fixed — the rate limiter is now keyed independently of widget lifecycle and covered by a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after — plus a second, defense-in-depth check added at resolve time and a test that keeps the UI-side allowlist mirror in sync with the server-side one. Nothing else from the review was left open.

The resulting safety story, concretely:
- **Rendering** is `allow-scripts` only — no `allow-same-origin`, so the iframe's origin is opaque and it can never touch the parent's storage, cookies, or DOM.
- **Serving** is static-file-only, path-jailed, and gated on registry approval status server-side — approval bypass isn't a client-trust question, it's enforced where the bytes are served from.
- **Networking** is structurally blocked (`connect-src 'none'` in the CSP), not just discouraged by convention.
- **Data** only ever reaches the widget through the bridge, resolved by the authenticated parent against the widget's own declared bindings — the widget itself never holds a credential and never talks to the gateway directly.
- **Prompt dispatch** is capability-gated in the manifest, confirm-dialog-gated per invocation, and rate-limited independent of the widget's mount/unmount lifecycle.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Agents cannot author bespoke widgets that render in the operator's dashboard, because running agent-authored HTML in the browser is unsafe without a hard sandbox. This PR adds the sandboxed custom-widget host: an `allow-scripts`-only iframe (opaque origin), a static-only, path-jailed, approval-gated serving route with `connect-src 'none'`, and a window-identity-filtered postMessage bridge where the trusted parent resolves the widget's declared bindings on its behalf — so an agent-scaffolded widget renders only after operator approval and never talks to the gateway directly.

**Evidence:** 79 plugin + 284 UI tests pass, including the path-jail suite (traversal, encoded traversal, absolute, backslash, symlink-out, name-charset, disallowed extension, non-GET → all 404 with `Content-Security-Policy` + `X-Content-Type-Options` asserted on every response), the bridge suite (foreign-window postMessage dropped, undeclared-binding denial, `sendPrompt` capability-gate + confirm dialog + rate limit), and the custom-widget E2E (approve → mount, a live `fetch()` from the widget blocked by CSP, the sandbox attribute asserted to be exactly `allow-scripts`, and the kill test). An independent adversarial review could not refute the path-jail, sandbox, or CSP across two passes and dozens of live probes; the one hole it found (a prompt rate limit that reset on widget remount) is fixed with a regression test that fails before and passes after. The scaffold → pending → approve → mount → live lifecycle is in the stills above and the recording.

## Verification

**Size:** ~1,400 lines of reviewable source across 9 files (the sandboxed-widget host) — comfortably inside VISION.md's ~5K reviewable-line guideline.

- Path-jail suite: traversal (`../`), encoded traversal, absolute paths, backslash variants, symlink-out, name-charset violations, disallowed extensions, non-GET requests — all 404, with correct `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Content-Type-Options` headers asserted on every response.
- Bridge suite: handshake, foreign-window postMessage correctly ignored, unknown message types dropped, undeclared binding requests denied, `sendPrompt` without capability denied without even showing a dialog, with capability shows the dialog and sends exactly once on confirm / nothing on deny, rate-limit behavior under remount.
- E2E: `connect-src 'none'` asserted against a live `fetch()` from inside a widget; sandbox attribute asserted to be exactly `allow-scripts` via DOM inspection; the kill test (a throwing widget produces an isolated error card, siblings and other tabs unaffected); the full approve → mount → live-update round trip against a fixture widget.
- The plugin serve/manifest/path-jail suites and the UI bridge + custom-widget suites pass (79 plugin + 284 UI tests), plus the custom-widget E2E (approve → mount, foreign-window drop, CSP `fetch()` block, sandbox-attribute assertion, kill test). CI runs on this PR.

## Closes / part of

Closes **#66983** / **#68497** (agent-rendered UI reachable from the browser — this is exactly that, with the safety work done up front). Partially addresses **#27574** (browser preview panel — the custom-widget host covers the "agent shows me something in the browser" half; a dedicated standalone preview panel outside the dashboard grid is not in scope here). Part of #101093. Builds on #101094, #101097 (top of the stack). With all three merged, the full end-to-end flow in the recording above — agent composes a tab, scaffolds and approves a sandboxed widget, live updates, human reorders — is reproducible against a running gateway.

target.title: Dashboard: widget write-back — persist widget state via a setState bridge capability
target.body:
> Give sandboxed widgets memory: a jailed, approval-gated `setState` capability that turns custom widgets from views into stateful apps.

Closes #101137. **Stacked on #101098** (the sandboxed custom-widget host) — that PR lands first; this targets `main` with a cumulative diff, so review the new `state`-related files as the delta.

## What problem this solves
Custom widgets today are read-only: the postMessage bridge lets a widget *ask* the parent for data, but there's no way to *save* anything — so an agent-built notes pad, kanban, or game resets on every reload. This adds the one missing primitive: per-widget, jailed, size-capped state, without loosening the sandbox.

## What's in this PR
- New gateway RPCs `dashboard.widget.state.get` / `.set` (read/write scoped), persisting to a path-jailed, size-capped per-widget file under `<stateDir>/dashboard/state/<widgetId>.json` — atomic writes, kept *separate* from `workspace.json` (does not count against the 256 KB workspace cap).
- New bridge inbound messages `dashboard:setState` / `getState`, gated behind a new `state:persist` manifest capability (mirrors the existing `sendPrompt` gate).
- The trusted parent resolves the widget's own `widgetId` — a widget can never read or write another widget's state, and a widget-supplied id is ignored.
- Unit tests covering the store round-trip (persist → read-back), the 64 KB size-cap whole-reject, widget-id charset/traversal rejects, the capability gate, read/write scope, and state-vs-workspace separation — the `extensions/dashboard` suite (85 tests) and the UI dashboard suite (94 tests) are green.
- This PR is the capability + its plumbing; the first shippable consumer is the stateful notes/todo widget (#101146), which depends on it.

## How it works
The design mirrors the read path from #101098: **the widget never holds a credential and never talks to the gateway** — the trusted Control-UI parent brokers everything. On `dashboard:setState`, the parent calls `dashboard.widget.state.set` with the `widgetId` *it* already tracks for that iframe (`widget.id`); the widget's message carries only the opaque blob, and the `setWidgetState` bridge dependency takes *only* the blob — there is no code path by which a widget names another widget's state. State is capped at **64 KB** per widget (the serialized envelope, rejected whole *before* any write), stored under `<stateDir>/dashboard/state/<widgetId>.json` (`0o700` dir / `0o600` file), serialized through the store's process mutex and written atomically via `replaceFileAtomic`. The widget id is charset-guarded (`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,48}$`) and the resolved path is re-checked for containment. The new `plugin.dashboard.widget-state.changed` broadcast carries `{ widgetId, version }` only — never the blob.

## Security
This widens the trust surface, so it carries the same adversarial-review discipline as #101098. Verified in code and tests:
- **(a) Own-state only** — the `widgetId` is always `widget.id`, bound by the trusted parent; the `setWidgetState` bridge dependency takes only the blob, and any id in the child's message is ignored.
- **(b) Size cap** — 64 KB enforced on the serialized envelope *before* any write; oversize is rejected whole (nothing written).
- **(c) Path jail** — the id is charset-guarded (`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,48}$`) and the resolved `state/<widgetId>.json` path is re-checked for containment.
- **(d) Capability gate** — `state:persist` is required; an ungated widget is denied *without touching the gateway*, the same shape as `sendPrompt`.
- **(e) No new iframe reach** — the iframe still cannot reach the gateway; the parent holds the socket and calls the new RPCs on the widget's behalf.
- **(f) Sandbox unchanged** — opaque origin, CSP `connect-src 'none'`, and the window-identity accept filter are all untouched.

Note: this PR adds **no new dependency** — `pnpm-lock.yaml` is unchanged, so the dependency-graph guard should not trip.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Sandboxed custom widgets cannot persist their own state (the bridge is read-only), so any agent- or user-built interactive widget resets on reload. This adds a jailed, size-capped, capability-gated `setState`/`getState` path so a widget can save and restore its own state.
**Evidence:** `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/dashboard` → 85 passed (store persist/read-back round-trip, 64 KB whole-reject, widget-id charset/traversal rejects, capability gate, read/write scope, and proof that widget state is written under `state/<widgetId>.json` and never into `workspace.json`); `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → 94 passed (bridge routes `setState`/`getState` only when the `state:persist` capability is present, and ignores any widget-supplied id); `pnpm ui:build` and oxlint clean.

target.title: fix(agents): avoid false unscheduled note after shell cron add
target.body:
Closes #52972

## What Problem This Solves

Shell-driven reminder creation could succeed through `openclaw cron add` while the turn still received the contradictory note that no reminder was scheduled.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reminder guard already records successful structured `cron` tool adds. This extends that producer-side evidence to successful direct OpenClaw CLI invocations made through `exec` or `bash`.

The classifier accepts the canonical `cron add` and `cron create` forms, root CLI options, executable paths, environment assignments, and explicit package executors such as `pnpm exec`, `pnpm dlx`, `npx`, and `bunx`. It uses the existing typed exec result contract and only counts a completed command with exit code 0.

To avoid false success, it rejects help-only calls, malformed shell input, bare pnpm package scripts, unrelated executables, and compound shell programs whose pipelines or control operators could mask the cron command's status. Portable redirections such as `2>&1` remain supported; bash-only `&>` forms are conservatively rejected because the exec shell may be POSIX `sh`.

## User Impact

Users no longer get a false unscheduled-reminder note after a supported shell cron add succeeds. Failed, masked, help-only, and unrelated commands still leave the guard active.

## Evidence

Exact PR head: `2a4fec68622ad7355a9d1883b80f8dd87073f474`

target.title: fix(chat): keep proof decision out of actor closure
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Swift 6.2 strict concurrency rejects `OpenClawChatSQLiteTranscriptCache.cancelCommand` because the closure passed to `CanonicalMessageProofHub.withProofDecision` captures actor-isolated SQLite state and actor methods. The failing diagnostic is `sending 'db' risks causing data races`, and it blocks `GatewayEndpointStoreTests`, the `OpenClaw` product build, and packaged app verification from current `main`.

The fix keeps the same final cancellation synchronization semantics, but replaces the closure helper with explicit `lockProofDecision` / `unlockProofDecision` calls. That keeps the final proof decision, SQLite commit, and cache removal inside the same synchronized region while leaving actor-isolated work in the actor method body.

## Summary

- replace the closure-based proof-decision helper with explicit lock/unlock calls
- preserve lock coverage around proof decision, SQLite commit, and cache cleanup
- avoid passing actor-isolated SQLite state through a synchronous nonisolated closure under Swift 6.2

target.title: Dashboard: inter-widget pub/sub — a tab-scoped, parent-brokered message bus
target.body:
> Widgets on the same tab can finally talk to each other — a filter widget drives a chart, a selector narrows a table — without ever being able to reach a widget on another tab.

Closes #101147. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `bus.ts` + the `bridge.ts` / host changes as the delta.

## What's in this PR
- Bridge messages `dashboard:publish` / `dashboard:subscribe` / `dashboard:unsubscribe` (inbound) delivering as `dashboard:message` (outbound), gated behind a new `bus:pubsub` manifest capability.
- A parent-brokered, DOM-free bus (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/bus.ts`): widgets never talk directly — the trusted parent fans a published payload out to the *other* same-tab subscribers on that channel.
- Caps: 8 KB payload, 60 publishes / 60 s (keyed by stable widget name so a remount can't reset the budget), 256-char channel names.

## Security model (this is the point of the design)
- **Tab isolation is structural, not a filter.** The subscription table is keyed `tabSlug → channel → subscriberId`, and a publish only ever iterates the *publisher's own tab bucket*. A widget on tab A cannot observe — or even enumerate — a subscriber on tab B; cross-tab delivery is unreachable code, not a rejected case.
- **Identity is broker-assigned.** The host mints an opaque `subscriberId` the widget never sees, and binds `tabSlug` from the widget's real tab (`tab.slug` in `renderGrid`) — both are closed over in the parent; a child message only ever carries an opaque `channel` + `payload`. A widget can't spoof another's identity, target a specific peer, or name a tab it wasn't assigned to. The publisher is excluded from its own broadcast.
- **No new reach.** The bus is in-memory and parent-brokered only — it never touches the gateway and never persists. The capability gate, size cap, and rate limit sit alongside the existing `sendPrompt` gates in `bridge.ts`; the `event.source` window-identity filter still guards the new inbound types; opaque origin unchanged.

All of the above is covered by tests (same-tab delivery, cross-tab non-delivery, publisher exclusion, capability denial both directions, size/rate caps, unmount teardown, unexpected-window rejection). No new dependency.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Dashboard widgets were fully isolated, so they couldn't compose — a filter widget had no way to drive a chart on the same tab. This adds a parent-brokered, tab-scoped pub/sub bus, capability-gated and rate/size-capped, with cross-tab isolation guaranteed by construction.
**Evidence:** `pnpm -C ui vitest run src/lib/dashboard src/components` green including the bus/bridge/host suites (tab-isolation, publisher-exclusion, capability gate, caps, unmount sweep); `pnpm ui:i18n:check`, `pnpm ui:build`, and full type-aware oxlint clean. Counts confirmed by the submitting orchestrator's own gate run (not agent-reported).

The bundled fallback and provider documentation contain only NVIDIA's current five featured models, while authenticated setup and model-selection paths continue pulling the live catalog from NVIDIA's static JSON feed.

### What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where NVIDIA Endpoint users could see outdated recommended models and metadata after NVIDIA updated its featured catalog.

## Changes

- Refresh the bundled NVIDIA fallback with Nemotron 3 Ultra, Nemotron 3 Super, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.6, and Minimax M3 using the values from NVIDIA's featured-model JSON.

- Extend NVIDIA catalog, onboarding, and registration tests for the refreshed rows.

### Why This Change Was Made

NVIDIA's public `featured-models.json` is the source of truth for current recommendations. OpenClaw already fetches that feed for authenticated setup and model selection; this change also aligns the bundled unavailable-feed fallback and documentation with the same source.

A widget can't spoof another's identity, target a specific peer, or name a tab it wasn't assigned to. The publisher is excluded from its own broadcast.
- **No new reach.** The bus is in-memory and parent-brokered only — it never touches the gateway and never persists. The capability gate, size cap, and rate limit sit alongside the existing `sendPrompt` gates in `bridge.ts`; the `event.source` window-identity filter still guards the new inbound types; opaque origin unchanged.

All of the above is covered by tests (same-tab delivery, cross-tab non-delivery, publisher exclusion, capability denial both directions, size/rate caps, unmount teardown, unexpected-window rejection). No new dependency.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Dashboard widgets were fully isolated, so they couldn't compose — a filter widget had no way to drive a chart on the same tab. This adds a parent-brokered, tab-scoped pub/sub bus, capability-gated and rate/size-capped, with cross-tab isolation guaranteed by construction.
**Evidence:** `pnpm -C ui vitest run src/lib/dashboard src/components` green including the bus/bridge/host suites (tab-isolation, publisher-exclusion, capability gate, caps, unmount sweep); `pnpm ui:i18n:check`, `pnpm ui:build`, and full type-aware oxlint clean. Counts confirmed by the submitting orchestrator's own gate run (not agent-reported).

target.title: Dashboard: stateful notes widget — the first consumer of widget write-back
target.body:
> A notes pad on your dashboard that actually saves — and the pattern every stateful builtin after it will follow.

Closes #101146. **Stacked on #101329 (widget write-back)**, which is itself stacked on #101098 — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `notes.ts` + the `buildBuiltinContext` host change as the delta beyond #101329.

## What's in this PR

- **`builtin:notes`** — an editable notes/todo pad. Content hydrates from persisted state on mount and saves on debounced input (~500 ms), so it survives reloads and stays consistent across two open browsers (the write-back broadcast triggers refetch).
- **A host-bound state accessor for builtins** — the piece that makes this safe and reusable. `BuiltinWidgetContext` gains an optional `state` accessor (`get`/`set`), and the dashboard view now builds the context **per widget** (`buildBuiltinContext`), closing over the host's own `widget.id` when it calls `dashboard.widget.state.get`/`.set`. A widget renderer never names a widget id — it can only ever touch its own state. This mirrors the trust model of the sandboxed path in #101329 (parent binds the id), applied to trusted builtins.
- **Graceful degradation** — with no connected client there's no `state` accessor, and the pad renders read-only with a hint instead of silently dropping writes.

## How it works
Builtins render in the trusted Control UI, so they use the write-back gateway RPCs directly rather than the sandbox's postMessage bridge — but the id-binding discipline is identical: the host supplies `widget.id`, never the renderer. The persist test drives the real `buildBuiltinContext` (not a hand-rolled mock) and asserts the RPC receives `{ widgetId: "notes-42", state: … }` — the id-binding itself is under test. State lives in the per-widget jailed store from #101329 (64 KB cap, atomic writes, separate from `workspace.json`).

No new dependency — `pnpm-lock.yaml` unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Operators want a scratchpad/todo on their dashboard, but before write-back (#101137/#101329) any editable widget reset on reload — and there was no pattern for a *builtin* to persist state safely. This adds a stateful notes builtin plus the host-bound per-widget state accessor that makes it (and future stateful builtins) possible.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → 98 passed, including the four new notes cases (editable render, hydrate from mocked `state.get`, debounced persist through the real host-built context asserting the host-bound `widget.id`, and the read-only no-client fallback); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and full type-aware oxlint clean.

target.title: Dashboard: ops widgets — agent status + approvals queue
target.body:
> The operational half of the builtin set: see what every agent is doing, and act on what's waiting for you — from a dashboard cell.

Closes #101145 and #101144. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `agent-status.ts` + `approvals.ts` and their wiring as the delta.

## What's in this PR

**`builtin:agent-status` (#101145)** — a compact per-agent/session status list: active-run vs idle, current label, and freshness — the "what's everything doing right now?" glance. It binds to the same `sessions.list` data the `sessions` builtin already uses (no new backend), so it live-updates on the existing broadcast path.

**`builtin:approvals` (#101144)** — a pending-approvals queue with Approve/Deny actions, wired end-to-end through the **existing** widget-approval infrastructure from #101098 (`dashboard.widget.approve`): pending `custom:` widgets appear as cards, and a decision dispatches the same client path the Workspaces pending-card uses. The queue arrives via a new `ctx.approvals` source on the builtin context (mirroring the existing `ctx.embed` pattern), because it's in-memory workspace state rather than an RPC binding.

**Scope note (deliberate):** the gateway's exec/plugin approval RPCs (`exec.approval.*`, `plugin.approval.*`) exist and the app shell uses them, but they are operator-scoped and not in the dashboard's read-only binding allowlist (`DATA_READ_RPC_ALLOWLIST`). Widening that allowlist is a security decision we didn't want to smuggle into a widget PR — so this widget covers the dashboard's own approval queue today, and is shaped to take exec/plugin approvals as additional sources the moment maintainers bless that allowlist addition (called out in the module header). That keeps #72545 progressing without expanding any privilege surface.

## How it works
Both widgets follow the established builtin contract (`renderX(widget, value, ctx) => TemplateResult`), registered in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS` + `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN`. Agent-status is a pure mapper over the resolved `sessions.list` value. Approvals renders from `ctx.approvals` (built by the dashboard view from workspace state) and dispatches decisions through the existing, already-authorized `dashboard.widget.approve` method — this PR adds **no new gateway method and no new privilege**.

No new dependency — `pnpm-lock.yaml` unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** There's no cross-agent activity view in the dashboard (#101145 / the #39127–#54577 cluster), and approvals had no dashboard surface (#101144, advancing #72545) — operators had to open each session or wait for the pending-card to appear on the Workspaces tab. This adds two operational builtins: a live agent-status list and an approvals queue with working Approve/Deny.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → 100 passed, including the new suites (status derivation filters + provenance, decision-vocabulary mapping + limit, populated/empty renders, and Approve/Deny wiring asserted against a mocked client dispatching `dashboard.widget.approve`); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and full type-aware oxlint clean; `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/dashboard` green (schema kind additions).

target.title: Dashboard: chart widgets + widget authoring SDK
target.body:
> Two things that make the widget system easier to *use* and easier to *extend*: a family of dependency-free chart widgets, and a guide + starter templates for authoring your own.

Closes #101142 and #101141. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review the new `chart.ts` + `docs/`/`examples/` files as the delta.

## What's in this PR

**Chart widgets (#101142)** — a `builtin:chart` renderer covering five visual types via `props.type`: `line`, `bar`, `area`, `sparkline`, `gauge`.
- Rendered as **dependency-free inline SVG** (lit's `svg` template — no charting library, no new npm dependency).
- Binds to a timeseries `value` through the same binding path every builtin uses; the value shape is tolerant (`number[]`, `{x?, y|value}[]`, or `{points:[…]}`) and normalized to a finite `number[]` before drawing.
- Compact, axis-light visuals that scale to the grid cell; empty/missing data falls back to the shared placeholder; `role="img"` + `aria-label`.

**Widget authoring SDK (#101141)** — `docs/plugins/dashboard-widget-authoring.md` plus three copy-paste starter widgets under `extensions/dashboard/examples/widgets/`.
- The guide documents **both** widget paths: builtin renderers (the `renderX(widget, value, ctx) => TemplateResult` contract, and registering a kind in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS` *and* `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN` — which must change together), and sandboxed custom widgets (the `widget.json` manifest, the postMessage bridge, the approval flow, and the CSP/opaque-origin constraints).
- Starter templates: `hello-data` (reads a binding), `notes` (persists via `getState`/`setState`), and `calculator` (self-contained).

## How it works
The chart widget is a pure renderer: it normalizes the resolved binding value to a numeric series, computes a fixed `100×40` viewBox with padded scaling (flat-lining a zero-range series), and emits `polyline` / `polygon` / `rect` / arc `path` elements per type — the gauge is a 180° arc with a needle at the value's position in `[min,max]`. Nothing fetches; the renderer only draws what its binding resolved. The SDK is documentation + example assets only — no runtime code changes.

Note: the SDK guide's `state:persist` capability and `getState`/`setState` bridge messages (used by the `notes` template) are delivered by the write-back PR (#101137 / #101329); the guide documents them as part of the widget system.

This PR adds **no new dependency** — `pnpm-lock.yaml` is unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** The dashboard had only stat-card and table builtins (no way to visualize a trend), and no documented path for contributors or agents to author new widgets. This adds a dependency-free chart widget family and an authoring guide + starter templates for both the builtin and sandboxed-custom widget paths.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → the UI dashboard suite is green (incl. the chart mapping/render suite: normalize shapes, per-type element counts for line/bar/area/gauge, and empty-state); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and oxlint clean. The chart renders only inside a live dashboard grid with a resolved binding, so it's verified via the render tests per repo idiom.

target.title: test(tooling): stabilize lifecycle measure pid fixtures
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`checks-node-core-tooling` can fail in the plugin lifecycle measure tests before the code under test is actually exercised. The Linux fixture reads temporary pid/ready files written by nested shell descendants. On a busy runner, the file path can be missing or still empty when the assertion reads it, and the `stubborn-descendant` fixture also used a 1s lifecycle timeout that can expire during nested process startup. The observed failure mode is `ENOENT` while reading `descendant.pid` in `test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts`.

This patch makes those fixtures wait for non-empty pid/ready files and gives the stubborn-descendant fixture enough startup budget while still verifying timeout cleanup and process-group termination.

## Summary

- wait for pid/ready fixture files to be non-empty before reading them in plugin lifecycle measure tests
- relax the stubborn-descendant phase timeout so Linux CI startup jitter does not race the fixture before it writes `descendant.pid`

## Evidence

Observed CI failure from a Linux `checks-node-core-tooling` run:

```text
FAIL test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts > plugin lifecycle resource sampler > kills stubborn descendants after the timeout grace period
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/tmp/openclaw-plugin-lifecycle-measure-.../descendant.pid'

FAIL test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts > plugin lifecycle resource sampler > forwards external termination to the measured process group
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/tmp/openclaw-plugin-lifecycle-measure-.../descendant.pid'
```

Linux after-fix CI proof on this PR:

- `checks-node-compact-small-whole-2` passed: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28111932652/job/83241443839
- The same Linux job ran `test/vitest/vitest.tooling.config.ts` and logged:

```text
test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts (12 tests) 4360ms
  kills stubborn descendants after the timeout grace period 3241ms
Test Files 278 passed | 1 skipped (279)
Tests 4413 passed | 15 skipped (4428)
[test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 296.34s
```

Full PR checks also passed after the body proof update, including `Real behavior proof`, `check-lint`, `check-test-types`, `check-prod-types`, and the Node compact shards.

Local verification on macOS:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.tooling.config.ts test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts --reporter=verbose
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  4 passed | 8 skipped (12)
```

Additional local checks:

```text

All matched files use the correct format.

# exit 0

node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-all.tsbuildinfo

```

Note: the lifecycle process-group assertions are Linux-only and are skipped on my local macOS host; the linked Linux CI job above covers the affected assertions after the patch.

target.title: feat(memory): carry source actor context into recall
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Memory recall can currently receive the conversation/session context without a stable indication of which group participant authored the triggering message. In multi-person channels, that can make retrieved or promoted memory read as if another participant's facts belong to the operator. This PR carries the generic source actor context into memory recall and prompt supplements so memory backends can preserve participant attribution without adding backend-specific logic.

## Summary

- Carries `SourceActor` from inbound context through embedded runs and plugin tool context.
- Exposes the same source actor context to memory corpus supplements for `memory_search` and `memory_get`.
- Reuses the typed `SourceActorRole` contract across reply runtime, plugin tool context, and memory context.
- Adds memory prompt/flush guidance to preserve participant attribution instead of merging another participant's facts into the operator/user profile.

## Scope and honesty

This PR carries `SourceActor` context into memory recall and adds prompt/flush guidance to preserve participant attribution. It is the plumbing + guidance layer: it makes attribution available and instructs the model to keep it. It does NOT yet structurally enforce attribution on stored memories (e.g., tagging persisted entries with the source actor) -- that is a follow-up. Best-effort: recall tracking never blocks recall.

## Stack

This is stacked after #96738, `codex/signal-mention-facts-context`, and `codex/source-actor-context-contract`. Until those land, this PR's diff will include its dependencies. Merge order should stay #96738 -> #96862 -> #96863 -> #96864, with later PRs rebased after earlier ones land.

## Diff shape

- Contract: source actor context and typed role reuse across reply/plugin/memory SDK types.
- Agent plumbing: inbound `SourceActor` is carried into embedded runs and plugin tool context.
- Memory core: `memory_search`/`memory_get` receive `sourceActor`; prompt/flush guidance mentions participant attribution.
- Signal prerequisite: mention context exposes delivered-turn mention facts only; skipped Signal turns do not create public prompt/tool context.
- Tests: channel/source actor parity, agent plugin context, auto-reply runner utils, memory-core source actor paths.
- Docs/API: channel plugin docs plus plugin SDK API baseline hash update.

## Production impact

No storage migration and no backend-specific behavior. This is not Honcho-specific: it adds a generic runtime/tool/memory contract that memory backends and supplements can consume. Core memory search still filters by existing session/source visibility; this PR does not claim a new per-person storage partition.

## Evidence

- Agent/tool context tests cover `SourceActor` propagation into plugin tool context.
- Auto-reply and inbound metadata tests cover carrying source actor context through reply runs.
- Memory-core tests cover source actor supplements in recall/citation paths and attribution guidance in memory output.
- Plugin SDK runtime mock tests cover `SourceActor*` parity with production inbound context.
- Plugin SDK API check passed after intentional baseline hash update:
  `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check`
- Focused tests passed:
  `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/channels/inbound-event/context.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/test-helpers/plugin-runtime-mock.test.ts extensions/signal/src/monitor/event-handler.mention-gating.test.ts extensions/memory-core/src/tools.citations.test.ts extensions/memory-core/index.test.ts src/agents/openclaw-tools.plugin-context.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-utils.test.ts`
- Production TypeScript check passed:
  `pnpm tsgo:prod`

### Redacted Runtime Proof

Temporary local proof harness imported production context/tool/memory code, registered a corpus supplement in-process, and executed `memory_search`/`memory_get` on PR head `3a4bbc94f0`. The proof preserves the source-actor plumbing facts while replacing all Signal identifiers, group identifiers, participant names, phone numbers, UUIDs, message bodies, and private memory keys with placeholders.

### Operational Signal group evidence (2026-06-26)

A private Signal group smoke was run after a production config hotfix that kept the group-bound agent responding without changing Docker permissions. The private runtime intentionally stayed on its deployed OpenClaw release instead of being advanced to this PR stack today; the facts below are operational evidence for the real Signal group route, not an additional claim that this PR head is live-deployed.

target.title: fix(signal): detect native bot mentions in group gating
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Signal groups can be configured with `requireMention=true` so side chatter stays quiet until the bot is explicitly mentioned. Signal native mentions arrive as structured `dataMessage.mentions[]` metadata plus object-replacement characters in the message text. The current Signal handler renders those placeholders as `@<uuid>` or `@<phone>`, then relies on text mention regexes. Selecting the bot from Signal's native mention UI can therefore fail to wake the bot unless a matching text fallback happens to be configured.

This also leaves `canDetectMention` tied only to configured text regexes and passes `hasAnyMention=false` even when Signal supplied structured mention metadata.

## Why This Change Was Made

This patch keeps the fix inside the Signal plugin and adds a small native mention fact resolver. It compares structured Signal mention metadata against the current bot account identity:

- UUID via `channels.signal.accountUuid`
- phone number via the existing E.164 normalizer and `channels.signal.account`

The event handler now combines text fallback and native metadata:

- `wasMentioned` is true for text fallback or a native mention that targets the current bot account.
- `canDetectMention` reflects text regexes or available bot account identity.
- `hasAnyMention` reflects valid structured Signal mention metadata so the shared mention-decision contract can distinguish command bypass from messages mentioning someone else.

Mentions of other participants do not trigger the bot. Missing bot identity does not become a false mention. Existing text fallback, group access checks, pending history, attachment restraint, control-command handling, direct messages, and `requireMention=false` behavior stay unchanged.

This supersedes #69413, which was closed without merge, by adding the missing capability facts, event-handler coverage, and docs.

## User Impact

Before:

> A user could select the bot from Signal's native mention UI in a `requireMention` group and get no response because the rendered `@uuid`/`@phone` text did not match the configured agent-name regex.

After:

> Native Signal mentions targeting the current bot account pass mention gating. Mentions of other participants remain silent and are kept only as bounded pending context. A later bot mention can include recent skipped group context and reply in the same group.

Docs now describe Signal native mention behavior, `accountUuid`, text mention fallback, and a mention-gated group configuration with bounded history.

### Behavior Change

Signal groups with `requireMention=true` that have a configured bot identity (`accountUuid`/`account`) but no text mention regexes previously fell through to pass-through handling. After this change they enforce mention gating via native Signal mention metadata. Group chatter that did not mention the bot but previously reached it may now be gated. This is intended and makes native-only `requireMention` groups behave as documented. Maintainers with such groups should expect stricter, correct gating after upgrade.

### Trust Model

`dataMessage.mentions[]` is sender-supplied. A group member could craft metadata naming the bot; the only effect is waking the bot, which any member can already do via a normal Signal mention. Native facts are still validated against a real object-replacement placeholder span, so malformed metadata does not become a bot mention.

### Native Identity Note

For full native mention coverage, configure `channels.signal.accountUuid` alongside `channels.signal.account`. Phone-only identity can still match phone-backed mention metadata, but UUID-only Signal mention metadata requires `accountUuid`.

## Evidence

- Base: `4ecb45b chore: update default check gate expectations`
- Head: `83ac15c979a4`
- Static whitespace check: `git diff --check HEAD~1..HEAD`
- Focused Signal mention-gating tests passed on this branch:
  `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/signal/src/monitor/event-handler.mention-gating.test.ts`
- Production TypeScript check passed:
  `pnpm tsgo:prod`

The focused Signal suite covers:

- native bot UUID mention without text mention patterns;
- native bot phone mention with E.164 normalization;
- native mention of another participant stays silent and records pending context;
- malformed matching metadata does not become a bot mention;
- no-detector behavior remains explicit;
- helper facts for bot mention, unrelated mention, malformed span, and missing bot identity.

### Redacted Live Signal Proof

This is the sanitized inspectable artifact from a live 3-person private Signal smoke. IDs, UUIDs, phone numbers, group IDs, raw message bodies, and private participant context are intentionally omitted.

```text
environment: live private Signal group
runtime: OpenClaw gateway with this PR's Signal mention patch installed
config.runtime: { signalConfigured: true, groupPolicy: "allowlist", groupAllowFromCount: 1, groupsCount: 1, requireMentionGroups: 1, accountUuidSet: true, historyLimit: 3 }
config.template: { signalConfigured: true, groupPolicy: "allowlist", groupAllowFromCount: 1, groupsCount: 1, requireMentionGroups: 1, accountUuidSet: true, historyLimit: 3 }
signal.probe: { configured: true, running: true, probeOk: true, probeStatus: 200 }
session.markerScan: { proofMarker: "96738", markerFileCount: 11, rawContentPrinted: false }

case: native bot mention from Signal UI

observed: bot account replied in the same group with the controlled proof marker

case: native non-bot participant mention from Signal UI
input: Signal native mention picker selected another group participant, not the bot
delivery: Signal message info showed delivery to both the bot account and the mentioned participant
expected PR facts: { canDetectMention: true, hasAnyMention: true, wasMentioned: false, shouldSkip: true }
observed: no bot reply was produced after the quiet window
```

- Restacked on current `main` after #99731 merged.
- Adds review-required `doctor --fix` previews for Gateway policy findings that should not be auto-mutated:

  - `policy/gateway-node-command-denied`: previews appending the missing command to `gateway.nodes.denyCommands`.
- Preserves skipped repair preview `changes` in the structured repair flow so review-required guidance is visible without counting the check as repaired.
- Documents the Gateway review-required preview behavior in `docs/cli/policy.md`; no generic Doctor docs were changed.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior or issue addressed:
`doctor --fix` surfaces review-required preview guidance for Gateway bind and Gateway node-command policy findings without mutating config or counting the check as repaired.

Real environment tested:
Windows PowerShell in `C:\src\openclaw-policy-review-previews-push`, source checkout at PR head `c4395e6`, rebased on current upstream `main`.

1. `git diff --check upstream/main..policy-doctor-review-required-previews`

3. `node scripts/check-docs-mdx.mjs docs/cli/policy.md docs/cli/doctor.md`
4. `pnpm docs:map:check`
5. `git diff --stat upstream/main..policy-doctor-review-required-previews`

The final PR diff is six files: gateway preview implementation/tests, repair-flow skipped-preview propagation, and one Policy doc paragraph documenting skipped non-mutating preview guidance for `policy/gateway-non-loopback-bind` and `policy/gateway-node-command-denied`.

target.title: fix(mobile): clarify gateway connection security setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Manual gateway setup on Android and iOS used ambiguous `Local` and `TLS` controls. Users could enter a remote hostname while the app still targeted loopback, select transport security without understanding the effective endpoint, or receive protocol/TLS failures without a concrete recovery step.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both mobile apps now:

- present connection security as `Unencrypted` or `Secure (TLS)`
- require secure transport for non-private hosts
- preview the effective `ws://` or `wss://` endpoint without replacing user-facing labels with protocol syntax
- provide actionable TLS guidance
- provide a copyable `openclaw update` command for gateway protocol mismatch

Remote-host security selection is deterministic local policy based on the entered host. It does not ping, probe, or otherwise preflight the gateway.

This PR is AI-assisted.

## User Impact

Android and iOS users get the same connection model and recovery guidance during onboarding and later manual gateway configuration. Remote connections can no longer silently retain a loopback-oriented mode, and error states explain the operator action needed to recover.

## Evidence

- Android focused unit tests and debug build passed.
- iOS focused tests passed: 23 tests, 0 failures.
- Fresh pre-commit `$autoreview` completed with no actionable findings.
- `git diff --check` passes on the rebased branch.
- Before/after screenshots are attached in the [mobile UI evidence comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101325#issuecomment-4899867668); no image assets are committed to the repository.

target.title: [AI-assisted] Add session history family lookup
target.body:
## Problem

When a threaded conversation has already been split across reset transcripts, `chat.history` and the `sessions_history` tool only read the currently active transcript. The session store can already retain the family through `usageFamilySessionIds`, but history readers do not use that chain and do not discover archived `*.jsonl.reset.<timestamp>` topic transcripts.

That means an agent/tool can be looking at the correct logical Telegram/Slack/Discord thread and still miss earlier turns after session rollover.

## Fix

Add an opt-in family history path:

- `chat.history` accepts `includeFamily: true`.
- `sessions_history` accepts `includeFamily`.
- Gateway and embedded `chat.history` now share the bounded/header-checked reset archive resolver instead of using separate prefix scans.
- The shared resolver can include owned topic-suffixed reset archives such as `<sessionId>-topic-456.jsonl.reset.<timestamp>` only when the archive header matches the requested session id.
- Same-prefix colliding topic archives and headerless topic archives are ignored.
- Family read targets are capped before transcript reads, and normal `chat.history` behavior remains opt-in: UI startup does not load ancestor history.

## Validation

Current head: `1aa4e9cbb94f6841803bd55559aa0ea6de17dc67`.

- `CI=true node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server.chat.gateway-server-chat-b.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.test.ts`
  - gateway shard: 84 tests passed
  - agents shard: 11 tests passed
- `CI=true node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/openclaw-tools.sessions.test.ts`
  - 36 tests passed
- `CI=true node --import tsx scripts/generate-prompt-snapshots.ts --check`
  - `Prompt snapshots are current (7 files).`
- `CI=true node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core-test.tsbuildinfo`
  - passed
- `CI=true node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo`
  - passed
- `git diff --check`
  - passed, no output

## Real Behavior Proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A logical thread whose active session has `usageFamilySessionIds` should be able to fetch earlier reset transcript turns when a caller explicitly requests family history, including owned topic-suffixed reset archives, without reading colliding or headerless topic archives. The current active transcript must also be preserved when a retained reset family has more entries than the bounded 32 read targets.
- **Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw checkout on this PR branch at current head `a12e1bbcf0`, using temporary on-disk session directories, the real Gateway `chat.history` RPC integration harness, embedded-mode `chat.history`, and the same reset archive filename/header patterns that OpenClaw creates for topic transcripts.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  1. Created temporary session directories and session-store entries with `usageFamilySessionIds` linking an ancestor session and the current session.
  2. Wrote an owned plain ancestor reset archive and an owned topic-suffixed ancestor archive with matching `type: "session"` headers.
  3. Wrote newer same-prefix colliding and headerless topic reset archives in the same sessions directory.
  4. Invoked the real Gateway `chat.history` RPC path with and without `includeFamily: true`.
  5. Created a second Gateway/RPC case with 40 ancestor session ids before the current id in `usageFamilySessionIds`.
  6. Invoked embedded-mode `chat.history(includeFamily)` through the sessions tool stub, including the same >32-family-target cap case.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture from current head:
  ```text
  $ CI=true node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server.chat.gateway-server-chat-b.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.test.ts
  Test Files  2 passed (2)
  Tests  84 passed (84)
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
  Tests  11 passed (11)
  [test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 44.69s

  $ CI=true node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/openclaw-tools.sessions.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
  Tests  36 passed (36)
  [test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 30.16s

  $ CI=true node --import tsx scripts/generate-prompt-snapshots.ts --check
  Prompt snapshots are current (7 files).

  $ CI=true node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core-test.tsbuildinfo
  # passed

  $ CI=true node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo
  # passed

  $ git diff --check
  # no output
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** Default `chat.history` excludes ancestor reset archive content, while `chat.history(includeFamily)` includes the owned plain ancestor archive, includes the owned topic-suffixed ancestor archive, includes current-session content, and rejects the colliding/headerless topic reset archives. In the >32-target Gateway/RPC regression, `chat.history(includeFamily)` contains `current survives family target cap`, contains early ancestor content, and does not read the ancestor entries beyond the target cap. Embedded `chat.history(includeFamily)` now reads the current active transcript first, then current archives, then ancestor archives/active transcripts; its >32-target regression also keeps the current transcript and drops over-cap ancestors.
- **What was not tested:** I did not run a live Telegram topic end-to-end, and this PR does not add prompt-level carryover summaries or automatic prompt injection. It only adds explicit family history retrieval for gateway/tool callers.

ClawSweeper's `a12e1bbcf0` review finding is addressed in this head:

- Family target selection still reserves the current active transcript before the 32-target cap is reached.
- Family output order is now ancestor transcripts first, then current-session reset archives, then the current active transcript, so final `limit` trimming keeps the active session tail.
- Embedded `chat.history(includeFamily)` mirrors the Gateway order.
- Added over-limit regressions proving `includeFamily` with a small final limit keeps current active history.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ACPX-backed MCP proxy sessions could crash with an unhandled stream error when the proxied target stdout stream emits an error.

The proxy already routes target stdin, proxy stdout, and child process errors through one controlled failure path. This change applies the same local boundary handling to the target stdout stream before piping it to the proxy stdout, without changing ACPX command rewriting or MCP payload behavior.

target.title: fix(web): avoid exact-limit fetch truncation warnings
target.body:
﻿Closes #101837

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `web_fetch` could see a response reported as truncated when the streamed response body was exactly `maxResponseBytes` bytes, even though no bytes were omitted.

## Why This Change Was Made

`readResponseText` now treats truncation as proven only when a chunk exceeds the remaining byte budget. Reaching the byte budget exactly no longer flips the truncation flag by itself, so exact-limit responses can complete normally while true overflow still cancels the reader.

## User Impact

Users no longer get misleading `Response body truncated after ... bytes.` warnings for complete responses that happen to land exactly on the byte cap. Oversized responses are still bounded and marked truncated.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: Current head `18b610b93e7e0a96de0eb891de3bab0e43f2c74b` lets an exact-limit `readResponseText` helper run complete without setting `truncated`, while still reporting the exact byte count.
- Real helper proof for the requested boundary, constructing a real `Response` from streamed chunks `"hello"` + `" world"` and reading it with `maxBytes: 11`:
  ```text
  node --import ../openclaw/node_modules/tsx/dist/esm/index.mjs --input-type=module -e "import { readResponseText } from './src/agents/tools/web-shared.ts'; const encoder = new TextEncoder(); let cancelCount = 0; const response = new Response(new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { controller.enqueue(encoder.encode('hello')); controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(' world')); controller.close(); }, cancel() { cancelCount += 1; } })); const result = await readResponseText(response, { maxBytes: 11 }); console.log(JSON.stringify({ text: result.text, truncated: result.truncated, bytesRead: result.bytesRead, cancelCount }));"
  {"text":"hello world","truncated":false,"bytesRead":11,"cancelCount":0}
  ```
- Focused regression: `PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR='../openclaw/node_modules' node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/web-shared.test.ts` passed (`1` file, `12` tests).
- Whitespace check: `git diff --check` passed.
- GitHub current-head checks: `gh pr checks 101845 --repo openclaw/openclaw --json name,bucket,state,completedAt,link` showed no failed buckets; current checks are pass/skip/neutral.
- Duplicate search before issue creation: no open issue or PR found for `web_fetch truncated maxBytes exact limit` or `readResponseText truncated maxBytes`.

Observed result: exact-limit helper output is `truncated:false`, `bytesRead:11`, and `cancelCount:0`, so the shared helper no longer feeds a false truncation warning to `web_fetch` for complete exact-cap responses.

## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. Agent `main`, local embedding provider, per-agent SQLite memory store at `~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite`. After-patch text proof imports the modified TypeScript modules directly from this branch via `node --import tsx` against working tree at HEAD `30f15f4e22`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

**Observed result after fix**: (a) The freshly written nested file `memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md` (two levels deep under `memory/`) was indexed by `openclaw memory index` and returned as the top match (score `0.812`) for the unique token.
